newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines welcomes credit rating upgrade.
newsitem.headline: Philippines welcomes credit rating upgrade.

text.p: The Philippines on Friday welcomed a long-awaited upgrade in the country's sovereign debt rating by international credit ratings agency Standard & Poor's Corp.

The upgrade for long-term foreign currency debt to BB-plus from BB and was attributed by S&P to improvements in public finances. Analysts said it brought the country a step closer to a highly regarded investment grade rating.
Analysts said the new rating should help the country achieve a more competitive price for its upcoming "Yankee" bond issue to be launched in U.S. markets in the second quarter.
U.S.-based S&P lifted ratings for the Philippines' peso-denominated debt to A-minus/A-1 from BBB-plus/A-2. It said the outlook for the country's long-term ratings was positive.
Some analysts said the country could receive an investment grade rating by May next year following presidential elections.

Officials and analysts said the news was expected and its immediate impact would improve the pricing of the Philippine Central Bank's maiden Yankee bond issue, expected to raise between $750 million to $1.0 billion.
A similar upgrade is also expected soon from Moody's Investors Service which announced three weeks ago that it was reviewing the Philippines for a possible upgrade.

"The Philippine Central Bank stands to immediately benefit from this development as it is set to issue its 30-year/100-year Yankee bonds very soon," Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said in a statement.
Analysts said the latest upgrade, however, would not have much of an impact on existing Philippine bonds.

"We haven't seen too much tightening in the secondary market because the upgrade was expected. It is just one more notch up the ladder for the Philippines, which has been trading up for a year," said Carlyle Peake, vice president at Merrill Lynch in Hong Kong.
He said many Philippine bonds already traded like issues with investment grade credit ratings.
S&P, however, warned that the country's ratings remained constrained by several factors, including the country's public sector's revenue base.
It said broadening the revenue base was essential to support adequate infrastructure development and reduce the share of non-discretionary expenses.
But analysts looked ahead to a further upgrade.

"Investment grade rating will not be that far away. The earliest will be after the (May) elections when the market has confirmed the qualified successor to President Ramos," said Noel Reyes, a trader of ING Bank in Manila.
But some thought it may come sooner.
"When we exit from the International Monetary Fund come June, we would have better chances to investment grade sooner than we expect," said Helen Alvarez, research head of All Asia Securities.

"The Philippine government is determined more than ever to complete its economic reform programme, permanently graduate from IMF conditional borrowing by June this year, and finally achieve investment-grade rating on its sovereign foreign currency debt," said Governor Singson in his statement.
The Philippines is optimistic that it can exit from 34 years of IMF supervision this year when it passes into law the remaining portion of a comprehensive tax reform package.
